title: Reinforcement Learning
premise: The lowest immediate employability of the deep track, and placed late on purpose rather than apologised for. Its value is that RLHF and reasoning-model training are built on it, and AIE-205 taught preference optimisation as a method without ever explaining the problem it was avoiding. This course explains the problem. By the end, DPO's whole appeal — that it removes the reinforcement learning — is something you can argue about rather than repeat.
why_here: Fourteenth of fifteen, and the ordering is a judgement rather than a prerequisite chain. Almost nothing in applied AI engineering requires it day to day, so it sits behind everything that does. It is here at all because a preference-optimisation pipeline you cannot connect to policy gradients is a recipe you follow rather than a technique you understand.
laboratory: Classic control environments on a laptop, and then your own AIE-205 checkpoints. The first half needs nothing but CPU — cart-pole and grid worlds are small enough to train in seconds and are the right size for watching an algorithm fail. The second half returns to the model you fine-tuned, which is where the abstractions stop being toys.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.
honesty_note: No advanced standing. Running DPO in AIE-205 evidences a library call, not an understanding of the objective it approximates.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: Reinforcement learning results are extremely seed-sensitive. Judges are instructed to treat a single-seed claim as unsupported regardless of how clean the curve looks, and to score a submission reporting high variance across seeds above one reporting a single tidy run.

items.title: The reinforcement learning problem
items.locator: Chapters 1 and 3 — the problem setting, then finite Markov decision processes, returns, and the value functions.

items.title: The framework, with code
items.locator: Unit 1 — the agent-environment loop and the reward hypothesis — and the introduction to the Bellman equation in unit 2.

items.title: Formalise something of your own as an MDP
checkpoints: A real decision problem chosen from your own systems
States, actions, transitions and rewards defined precisely
The discount factor chosen with a stated justification
One property of the formalisation shown to be false in reality
items.brief: Take a real decision problem from one of your own products — which model to route a request to, when to re-index, how many retrieval results to fetch — and formalise it as an MDP. Define the state, action and reward precisely enough that someone else could implement it. Choose a discount factor and justify it in terms of the actual decision horizon rather than by using 0.99 because everyone does. Then name one place where the Markov property does not hold in reality, because that is almost always true and pretending otherwise is where applied RL goes wrong.

items.title: Where the framing breaks
checkpoints: Partial observability identified concretely in the chosen problem
The consequence for a learned policy stated
A reformulation attempted
A judgement recorded on whether RL is the right tool at all
items.brief: Take the MDP you just wrote and attack it. Where is the state only partially observable? Where does the reward arrive so late that credit assignment becomes hopeless? Where would exploration be unacceptable because it means giving real users bad answers? Attempt a reformulation. Then record the judgement this course wants you to be able to make: given all that, is reinforcement learning the right tool for this problem, and if not, what is.

items.title: Dynamic programming, before learning
items.locator: Chapter 4 — policy evaluation, policy improvement and policy iteration, with the model known. Everything later is this without the model.

items.title: Monte Carlo and temporal difference
items.locator: Chapters 5 and 6 — Monte Carlo prediction and control, then TD learning, SARSA and Q-learning.

items.title: Q-learning and deep Q-networks
items.locator: Units 2 and 3 — tabular Q-learning, then the deep Q-network and the tricks that make it work.

items.title: Tabular Q-learning from the update rule
checkpoints: The update rule written out before the code
Implemented on a small environment and converging
Exploration schedule chosen and its effect shown
Learned value function inspected against intuition
items.brief: Implement tabular Q-learning on a small environment from the update rule as written in the book, not from an example. Get it to converge. Then vary the exploration schedule and show what happens with too little exploration — the agent finds a mediocre policy and stops, confidently. Finally, print the learned value function and check it against what you would expect: states near the goal should be worth more, and if they are not, something is wrong that the reward curve did not tell you.

items.title: Break it with function approximation
checkpoints: The tabular version replaced with a function approximator
Instability produced and its signature recorded
One of the three destabilising ingredients removed and re-measured
The deadly triad named in terms of what was observed
items.brief: Replace your table with a neural network and watch it become unstable. Record what that looks like — diverging values, oscillation, catastrophic forgetting of an earlier good policy. Then remove one leg of the deadly triad: use on-policy data, or drop bootstrapping, or add a target network to slow the moving target. Measure the difference. The claim to defend is which ingredient you removed and why that specific one addressed what you actually saw.

items.title: The taxonomy of algorithms
items.locator: Part 2, Kinds of RL Algorithms — the model-free split between policy optimisation and Q-learning, and what each trades away.

items.title: Retention: value methods and the deadly triad
Intro to policy optimisation
items.locator: Part 3, Intro to Policy Optimization — the derivation of the simplest policy gradient, line by line, including why the log appears.

items.title: The policy gradient theorem
items.locator: Chapter 13 — the policy gradient theorem, REINFORCE, REINFORCE with baseline, and actor-critic.

items.title: REINFORCE, from the derivation
checkpoints: The gradient estimator derived in the submission
Implemented and learning on a small environment
At least five seeds run
Spread across seeds reported alongside the mean
items.brief: Derive the REINFORCE estimator in your own writing, then implement it. Train on a small control task. Run at least five seeds and plot all of them, not the mean alone — reinforcement learning curves are famously seed-sensitive, and a single run is a screenshot rather than a result. Report the spread. If two seeds solve the task and three never learn, that is the finding and it is entirely normal.

items.title: Variance reduction, measured
checkpoints: Gradient variance measured directly, not inferred from the reward curve
A baseline added and variance re-measured
Sample efficiency compared at equal environment steps
The bias question addressed
items.brief: Measure the variance of your gradient estimates directly rather than inferring it from how wobbly the reward curve looks. Add a baseline — a learned value function, or even a running mean of returns — and measure the variance again. Compare sample efficiency at equal environment steps rather than equal wall-clock. Then answer the question that makes the baseline legitimate: why does subtracting it not bias the estimator.

items.title: Reference implementations, afterwards
items.locator: The vpg and ppo implementations — read only after your own REINFORCE works, and read for the engineering details the derivations omit.

modules.title: From policy optimisation to preference optimisation

items.title: InstructGPT, as a reinforcement learning paper
The PPO trainer, against the DPO one
items.locator: The PPO trainer, read directly against the DPO trainer you used in AIE-205 — the interesting content is everything PPO needs that DPO does not.

items.title: Where the reward actually lands
checkpoints: The RLHF setup mapped onto the MDP vocabulary from M1
The credit assignment problem stated concretely for token generation
The KL penalty's role identified in RL terms
One consequence for behaviour predicted and checked against the literature
items.brief: Map RLHF onto the MDP vocabulary you learned in M1: what is the state, what is the action, when does the reward arrive. Then state the credit assignment problem precisely — a single scalar at the end of a sequence has to explain every token choice. Identify what the KL penalty is doing in reinforcement learning terms rather than as a regularisation trick. Finish by predicting one behavioural consequence and checking it against what the papers report.

items.title: Why DPO gets to skip all this
checkpoints: The DPO objective related to the RLHF objective it approximates
The assumption that permits the reparameterisation identified
A case constructed where that assumption is questionable
A position taken on when PPO-style RLHF is still worth its cost
items.brief: You ran DPO in AIE-205 as a method. Now explain what it is doing: it reparameterises the RLHF objective so the reward model disappears and the optimisation becomes supervised. Identify the assumption that makes this legal. Then construct a case where that assumption is questionable, and take a position — with reasons — on when the full PPO pipeline is still worth its considerable extra cost. This is the item that retroactively justifies putting this course in the programme.

items.title: PPO, as documented
items.locator: The PPO page — the objective, the clipping, and the pseudocode.

items.title: Retention: RLHF and its relation to DPO
rlhf-study, published
checkpoints: The policy-gradient implementation published with its seed spread
The written account of reward hacking included
The DPO-versus-PPO argument stated as a position, not a summary
Connected backwards to AIE-205
items.brief: Publish the study the reinforcement-learning capability points at: your policy-gradient implementation with its honest seed spread, the reward-hacking failure you produced, and your position on when preference optimisation is enough. It must connect backwards to AIE-205, because the whole argument of this course is that the method you used there is an approximation to something, and this is where you say to what.

items.title: Make it hack the reward
checkpoints: A reward function written with a plausible flaw
An agent trained that exploits it
The exploit described and its reward accounted for
The reward repaired and the new exploit found, or its absence argued
items.brief: Write a reward function that looks reasonable and contains an exploitable flaw, then train an agent until it finds the exploit. Describe what it did and show the reward it obtained. Then repair the reward and try again. The second round is the point: reward specifications are usually broken in more than one way, and the experience of fixing one and immediately finding another is the thing that transfers to writing evaluation criteria for anything, including the rubrics in this programme.

items.title: Actor-critic and PPO in practice
items.locator: The advantage actor-critic and PPO units, including the practical notes on what breaks in real training runs.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your own submissions at defense time, answered aloud without notes. This defense carries the reinforcement-learning capability claim.
sample_question_shapes: Three of your five seeds never learned. A reader says the method does not work. Answer them.
Explain, without saying the words 'policy gradient', why subtracting a baseline does not bias the estimator.
You argued DPO is enough for most cases. Give me the strongest case against your own position.

items.title: What remains unsolved
items.locator: Chapter 17 — the frontiers section, read for the problems that are still open rather than for technique.

rubrics.integrity: This defense carries the reinforcement-learning capability claim. A candidate who can state the strongest case against their own conclusion scores higher than one who defends it uniformly.

completion.required: All eight assignments, the project and the defense submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on all four reinforcement-learning skills, which makes the last unclaimable area claimable and completes the programme's coverage. FSRS then decays them.
